Oh, I suspected this, actually. So, with this method you can't do a sighted solve without memorizing first because you may run into two issues: Parity and Special Targets.

With this method, the four targets on the middle layer abide by a special rule: If they come second in a letter pair, you must do the inverse algorithm instead of the regular one (i.e.: BU instead of UB, DB instead of BD).

This happens because the first letter of this pair (whichever it is) will offset the middle layer by 2, and then those pieces are positioned inverse to one another. Doing the inverse algorithm at the second letter of this pair will fix that, and the middle layer will end up fixed.

What I did when learning this method was writing down the memo and then doing a sighted solve following it to see how the cube would end up affected after each letter. If at the end you don't end up with a solved cube, you will be able to backtrack what you missed.

Also, I suggest using edge-only scrambles for this. You won't run into Parity but the special cases might show up.

LL optimization comes in many flavors, and it depends on the situation. Overall top speedcubers know subsets like COLL, VHLS, some ZBLL cases and pair them up with Edge Control and similar cubic techniques. 

However, their one singular meeting point is lookahead.

The marginal advantages provided by magnets and finer tuning are only really perceivable by competitive solvers who are already at the top of their game, or at least deeply invested in the hobby. Those individuals likely already know how to optimally set up their equipment, or have so much invested into the pastime that purchasing a custom puzzle is not a hassle.

It's also worth mentioning that custom equipment has a subjective expiration date - lubrication wears off and tensions don't remain exactly the same as originally set up forever. Not to mention other very subjective "feeling factors" are prone to change over time and even in distinct situations, regardless of the time frame (i.e.: warming up).

For perspective: While it is a fact that a professionally set up and maintained high-end guitar would allow me to become an objectively better guitarist faster than my reliable older model ever could, I won't catch up to top professionals unless I earn my keep through extensive practice. And while those professionals could objectively play just as well on my guitar as they do with their own, using their own equipment is the edge they need to break through the sound barrier.

Also consider the following: There is an acceptable possibility that current top competitive solvers reached their current standings in the world rankings partially because of their respective "back in the day" hardware limitations.

For 3Style algorithms, it's primarily about execution. Once I feel comfortable with it, I will do a few slow repetitions just to track the pieces as they move around, which helps me understand and visualize what the algorithm does.

In my opinion, this is an important step in learning algorithms because if I make a mistake during a solve, it's easier to backtrack. Additionally, if I happen to forget how to execute it, I can quickly improvise from a different algorithm.

For instance, if I forget how to perform the cycle involving specific pieces, instead of panicking and resorting to a much slower solution, I would simply set up with a different move into the algorithm for another cycle (which happens to be very fast as well, so if my think-ahead is good, the loss in actual execution time is minimal).
